title: (Scenario) A dependency has 99.9% availability but your API is expected to provide 99.99% — is that possible, and how (not if every successful request requires that dependency synchronously — you must remove the dependency from some critical request paths via caching, replication, async workflows, or degraded functionality) — and why must availability targets be translated into concrete behavior rather than SLA numbers alone?
shortTitle: A dependency has 99.9% availability but your API needs 99.99% — is that possible, and how?

s1_definition.profdef: If every successful request synchronously requires a dependency, your API's availability cannot exceed that dependency's availability — a 99.9% dependency caps a synchronous caller at 99.9%, so a 99.99% target is mathematically impossible on that path. Achieving a higher availability than a dependency requires removing the dependency from the critical path for at least some requests, through caching (serve from cache when the dependency is down), replication (multiple independent instances whose combined availability exceeds any single one), asynchronous workflows (accept the request durably and complete the dependency interaction later), or degraded functionality (return a reduced-but-valid response when the dependency is unavailable). Availability targets must be translated into these concrete behaviors because an SLA number alone does not tell you what the system actually does when the dependency fails; only the behavior determines whether the target is met.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India promises customers that balance checks succeed 99.99% of the time, but the central mainframe it queries is only up 99.9% of the time. If every balance check must phone the mainframe and wait, the bank can never beat the mainframe's uptime — its promise is impossible. So the bank changes what a balance check actually does: it keeps a recent copy of balances at the branch (caching) so it can answer when the mainframe is down, it connects to two mainframes instead of one (replication), or it tells the customer "here is your balance as of a minute ago" when the live system is unreachable (degraded functionality). The promise is kept not by a better number on paper but by changing the behavior so the mainframe is no longer on the critical path for every check.
s1_definition.oneliner: You cannot exceed a synchronous dependency's availability — to beat it, remove it from the critical path via caching, replication, async, or degradation, and express the target as concrete behavior, not just an SLA number.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** If every successful request synchronously requires a dependency, your API's availability cannot exceed that dependency's availability — a 99.9% dependency caps a synchronous caller at 99.9%, so a 99.99% target is mathematically impossible on that path. Achieving a higher availability than a dependency requires removing the dependency from the critical path for at least some requests, through caching (serve from cache when the dependency is down), replication (multiple independent instances whose combined availability exceeds any single one), asynchronous workflows (accept the request durably and complete the dependency interaction later), or degraded functionality (return a reduced-but-valid response when the dependency is unavailable). Availability targets must be translated into these concrete behaviors because an SLA number alone does not tell you what the system actually does when the dependency fails; only the behavior determines whether the target is met.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India promises customers that balance checks succeed 99.99% of the time, but the central mainframe it queries is only up 99.9% of the time. If every balance check must phone the mainframe and wait, the bank can never beat the mainframe's uptime — its promise is impossible. So the bank changes what a balance check actually does: it keeps a recent copy of balances at the branch (caching) so it can answer when the mainframe is down, it connects to two mainframes instead of one (replication), or it tells the customer "here is your balance as of a minute ago" when the live system is unreachable (degraded functionality). The promise is kept not by a better number on paper but by changing the behavior so the mainframe is no longer on the critical path for every check.

**One line to remember:** You cannot exceed a synchronous dependency's availability — to beat it, remove it from the critical path via caching, replication, async, or degradation, and express the target as concrete behavior, not just an SLA number.

sections.s2_technical:
The math is unforgiving. Availability composes multiplicatively along a synchronous critical path: if your API must call a dependency on every request and succeed, your availability is at most the dependency's availability, and if you depend on several such dependencies, you multiply their availabilities together, so it only gets worse. A 99.9% dependency means about 8.76 hours of downtime per year; a 99.99% target means about 52.6 minutes. You cannot promise 52 minutes of downtime while sitting behind something that is down for nearly 9 hours, if every request needs it. So the first thing I say is: on a purely synchronous path, no, it is not possible — the target is a contradiction.

The way out is to make the dependency non-essential for some requests. Caching is the most common technique: you keep recent results so that when the dependency is unavailable, you serve from cache. During the dependency's downtime, cached reads still succeed, so your read availability is decoupled from the dependency's. The trade-off is staleness — you are serving data that may be slightly old — which is why this works for balance display but not for the authoritative debit decision.

Replication raises the dependency's own effective availability. If the dependency is a single instance at 99.9%, running multiple independent replicas and failing over between them makes the probability that all are down far smaller — two independent 99.9% replicas give roughly 99.9999% combined, because both must fail simultaneously. The key word is independent: replicas sharing a single point of failure do not help. This turns the dependency itself into something reliable enough to sit on the critical path.

Asynchronous workflows remove the dependency from the synchronous success path entirely. Instead of calling the dependency and waiting, you durably accept the request — write it to a log or queue — and return success immediately, then complete the dependency interaction in the background with retries. The user's request succeeds as soon as it is safely recorded, so the API's availability depends on the durable accept, not on the dependency being up at that instant. This fits writes and commands that do not need the dependency's result synchronously, like submitting a transfer that settles asynchronously.

Degraded functionality keeps the API available with a reduced response when the dependency is down. If a recommendation service that normally enriches a response is unavailable, you return the core response without recommendations rather than failing. The request still succeeds against its core contract, so availability is preserved, as long as you define the degraded response as a valid success rather than an error.

The reason targets must be translated into concrete behavior is that the number alone is empty. "99.99%" does not tell an engineer what to build; "when the fraud dependency is down, transfers up to fifty thousand rupees are approved from cached risk scores and larger ones are queued for async review" does. The behavior is what you implement, test, and verify, and it is the behavior that determines whether the number is actually achieved. Two systems can both claim 99.99% while one falls over the moment its dependency hiccups and the other degrades gracefully; the SLA number hides that difference, and only the specified behavior reveals it. So I convert every availability target into statements of the form "when dependency X is unavailable, request type Y still succeeds by doing Z," and then I test those statements by injecting the dependency's failure.

The senior nuance is that not every request can be decoupled, and you must be honest about which ones cannot. The authoritative debit of an account genuinely needs the source of truth, so for that specific operation you may not be able to beat the dependency's availability, and the right answer is to raise the dependency's availability through replication rather than to pretend caching makes a stale balance authoritative. So the overall API target is met per request type: reads hit a high number via caching, async commands via durable accept, and the few truly synchronous critical operations via a replicated, hardened dependency.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India the balance API must provide 99.99% availability, but the core-ledger dependency it reads is only 99.9%.

Problem 1 — the original design calls the ledger synchronously on every balance read, so the API can never exceed 99.9% — the target is mathematically impossible. This is exactly why a synchronous dependency caps the caller's availability.

Problem 2 — the fix for reads is caching: recent balances are cached, so when the ledger is down the API serves the cached balance marked as slightly stale, keeping read availability high and decoupled from the ledger. This is exactly caching plus degraded functionality.

Problem 3 — transfers, which are writes, are made asynchronous: the API durably accepts the transfer and returns success immediately, settling against the ledger in the background with retries, so transfer-submission availability depends on the durable accept, not the ledger being up. And the one truly synchronous operation — an authoritative debit check — is backed by a replicated ledger to raise its own availability. This is exactly async workflows and replication.

The demo models the ledger with 99.9% availability, runs balance reads through a cache-with-degradation path and transfer submissions through an async-accept path while the ledger flaps, and reports the achieved availability per request type to show 99.99% is reached off a 99.9% dependency.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one hundred thousand balance reads and one hundred thousand transfer submissions against a core-ledger dependency that is only 99.9% available, meaning roughly one in a thousand ledger calls fails.

Step 1: The cache is warmed with one successful read, so a recent balance is available to serve during any ledger outage.

Step 2: Each balance read tries the ledger first. About 99.9% of the time the ledger responds, the response is fresh, and the cache is refreshed. The remaining roughly one in a thousand times the ledger is down.

Step 3: On a ledger failure the read path does not fail — it serves the cached balance marked as stale, which is a valid, successful, degraded response. So a read succeeds whether the ledger is up (fresh) or down (stale), which decouples read availability from the ledger. Measured read success exceeds 99.99%, because a read only truly fails in the vanishing case of both a ledger outage and a cold cache.

Step 4: Each transfer submission writes the request durably to the inbox and returns accepted immediately, without calling the ledger synchronously. Settlement happens later in the background with retries, so submission success depends only on the durable accept, which essentially always succeeds. Measured write availability exceeds 99.99%.

Step 5: The demo reports both availabilities, each above the 99.99% target even though the dependency is only 99.9%. The point it prints is that the target was achieved not by any paper SLA but by concrete behavior — caching with degradation for reads and durable async accept for writes — that removed the dependency from the synchronous success path.

```
2026-10-24 19:05:13 [INFO] Read availability (cache+degrade) = 100.0000%
2026-10-24 19:05:13 [INFO] Write availability (async accept)  = 100.0000%
2026-10-24 19:05:13 [INFO] Both exceed 99.99% off a 99.9% dependency — target achieved by BEHAVIOR
```

```
  TRULY SYNC op (authoritative debit) ──▶ cannot beat dep → REPLICATE ledger
       two independent 99.9% replicas → ~99.9999% combined
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
My first answer is a piece of math: if every successful request synchronously requires a dependency, your availability cannot exceed that dependency's availability. A 99.9% dependency caps a synchronous caller at 99.9%, which is about nine hours of downtime a year, so a 99.99% target — about fifty-three minutes a year — is simply impossible on that path. If you depend on several such dependencies synchronously, you multiply their availabilities and it gets worse. So on a purely synchronous critical path, the honest answer is no, the target is a contradiction.

The way to actually beat the dependency is to remove it from the critical path for at least some requests, and there are four concrete techniques. Caching lets you serve recent results when the dependency is down, so read availability is decoupled from the dependency at the cost of some staleness — right for balance display, wrong for an authoritative debit. Replication raises the dependency's own effective availability: two independent 99.9% replicas with failover give roughly 99.9999% combined, because both must be down at once, and the word independent is critical, because replicas sharing one failure point do not help. Asynchronous workflows remove the dependency from the synchronous success path entirely — you durably accept the request and return success immediately, then complete the dependency interaction in the background with retries, so your availability depends on the durable accept, not on the dependency being up at that instant. Degraded functionality keeps the API available with a reduced-but-valid response when the dependency is down, as long as you define that degraded response as a success rather than an error.

The reason targets must be translated into concrete behavior, rather than left as SLA numbers, is that the number alone is empty and even misleading. "99.99%" tells an engineer nothing about what to build; "when the ledger is down, balance reads serve the last cached value marked stale, and transfer submissions are durably accepted and settled asynchronously" tells them exactly what to build, test, and verify. Two systems can both claim 99.99% while one collapses the moment its dependency hiccups and the other degrades gracefully — the number hides that difference, and only the behavior reveals it. So I convert every availability target into statements of the form "when dependency X is unavailable, request type Y still succeeds by doing Z," and then I prove each one by injecting the dependency's failure and measuring.

The senior nuance I always add is honesty about the requests you cannot decouple. The authoritative debit of an account genuinely needs the source of truth, so for that specific operation you cannot pretend a stale cache is authoritative — the right move there is to raise the dependency's availability through independent replication, not to fake it. So the overall API target is met per request type: reads reach the high number via caching and degradation, async commands via durable accept, and the few truly synchronous critical operations via a replicated, hardened dependency.

In my banking work this was exactly how we delivered a 99.99% balance API on top of a 99.9% core ledger. Reads went through a cache that served a stale-but-valid balance during ledger outages, transfers were durably accepted and settled asynchronously so submission never waited on the ledger, and the one genuinely synchronous authoritative check was backed by a replicated ledger. We wrote the target as behavior per request type and verified it by deliberately taking the ledger down in tests, which proved the API stayed available well above its target even though the dependency underneath it never improved beyond 99.9%.
